newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Allianz says Holocaust suit impact unclear.
newsitem.headline: German Allianz says Holocaust suit impact unclear.

text.p: FRANKFURT, April 2 - German insurance giant Allianz AG Holding on Wednesday said the implications of a U.S. lawsuit by Holocaust survivors who say European insurers cheated them of billions of dollars were as yet unclear.
Its comment on the lawsuit filed in Manhattan Federal Court on Monday was based on its own initial examinations.

The lawsuit alleges that Allianz and other defendants "with a reputation for confidentiality and professionalism" encouraged European citizens who feared persecution by the Nazis to deposit their assets with them and to purchase insurance to safeguard their family's futures.

In the class action suit combining the complaints of numerous plaintiffs, the Holocaust victims and their families allege that the insurers then withheld, concealed or converted the cash value and proceeds of policies sold prior to 1946.

"Being Germany's largest insurance company, everyone will look at Allianz, but there is no direct connection between any of the cases in the suit and Allianz that seems to make sense," Allianz spokesman Christopher Worthley told Reuters.
Allianz has made payments in similar cases in the past but there are currently no open cases, he said.
When claims were made against Allianz policies, all legitimate cases were paid. He was unable to specify the amount paid out to date.
Allianz said that it had yet to receive a complete official copy of the lawsuit but had received details by fax from the United States on request.
"We are affected by this as we are named as defendants but the cases where Allianz is mentioned are few," Worthley said.
"We take this complex issue extremely seriously and will be busy looking at it but in terms of the actual content, it is very difficult to say anything yet," he added.
The suit estimates that the class of plaintiffs would exceed 10,000 members and seeks billions of dollars in damages to be determined at trial.
A prominent member of the German Jewish community said that if there was any question of wrongdoing by the insurance industry relating to the Nazi era, then that had to be exposed.

"I think it is important that legal authorities also seek to uncover immoral behaviour by industry and companies during the Third Reich," said Michel Friedman, executive board member of the Central Council of Jews in Germany.

"Banks and insurers bear a high level of responsibility for their own credibility and moral integrity. If insurers profited from the Holocaust, then the courts have to be aggressive in exposing the truth," said Friedman.
Allianz chief Henning Schulte-Noelle has said in speeches that it has to hold itself accountable for its entire corporate history, including the years between 1933 and 1945.
There are gaps in Allianz's records which it said it is trying to rectify and the group does not rule out bringing in a historian to accomplish this task.
Among the other insurers named in the suit is Wiener Allianz, an Allianz unit.

This allegation would be dealt with accordingly, Allianz said, adding that Wiener Allianz only acquired the name in 1938 and only began writing life insurance in 1960 and there could be a case of mistaken identity.

Other defendants in the case include Assicurazioni Generali S.p.A. of Trieste, Italy, A.G.F. Assurances Generales de France Vie of Paris, Riunione Adriatica Di Sicurta S.p.A. of Milan and Bavarian Reinsurance Co of Munich.
